---
title: "Testing the whole tree"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 5)
```

`node_test()` asks which clades respond to the environment. Peres-Neto & Kembel (2015)
proposed two frameworks that ask whether phylogenetic composition follows the environment
across the whole tree, and both are in the package. The results below are simulated.

```{r}
library(comdynamite)

set.seed(1)
tree <- treeshapesim::sim_tree_shape(20)
traits <- species_traits(tree, lambda = 1, optima_range = c(-1, 101), rmax_range = c(0, 30))
env <- runif(50, 0, 100)
comm <- simulate_static(traits, env, incidence = TRUE)$abundance
keep <- rowSums(comm) > 0
comm <- comm[keep, ]
env <- env[keep]
```

## Phylogenetic community composition

`pcc_test()` takes the principal coordinates of the distances among species, averages them
within sites, and regresses each average on the predictors. The test statistic is the variance
of the adjusted R2 across eigenvectors, and the value to report is the mean of the positive
adjusted R2.

```{r}
pcc <- pcc_test(comm, tree, env, n_perm = 199)
pcc
```

## Phylogenetic beta diversity

`phylo_beta_test()` starts from the distance between communities given by `phylo_beta()`, the
mean phylogenetic distance between their species, and fits a distance-based redundancy
analysis.

```{r}
beta <- phylo_beta_test(comm, tree, env, n_perm = 199)
beta
```

`scores` holds the sites on the principal coordinates of the predicted matrix, which the
authors suggest using to order sites in a heatmap of the community matrix. `plot_phylo_beta()`
draws it, with species in the order of the tree, so that clades replace each other along the
sites when composition follows the environment.

```{r}
plot_phylo_beta(beta, comm, tree)
```

## Principal coordinates of phylogenetic structure

`pcps_test()` computes the principal coordinates of phylogenetic structure (Duarte 2011; Duarte
et al. 2016), the method of the package PCPS (Debastiani & Duarte 2014). By phylogenetic fuzzy
weighting (Pillar & Duarte 2010), each species shares its relative abundance with its relatives,
in proportion to their similarity on the tree, and the principal coordinates of the resulting
matrix order sites by phylogenetic composition. The test covers all the
dissimilarity and, separately, each axis in `axes`, whose `share` is its part of the variation.

```{r}
pcps <- pcps_test(comm, tree, env, n_perm = 199)
pcps
```

Unlike the method of `pcc_test()`, which works on eigenvectors of the tree, this one takes
eigenvectors of the sites, so `scores` can be plotted against the environment. `plot()` draws
the sites on the first two axes, coloured by the environment, with each species as an arrow
from the correlation of its column of the matrix P with the axes.

```{r, eval = requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)}
plot(pcps)
```

With many species the arrows are hard to read. `clades` draws the species as stars grouped
into clades instead, either the k deepest clades of the tree or groups given by name, such as
families, as in Fig. 1 of Debastiani & Duarte (2014). The plot then shows which lineages go
with which sites.

```{r, eval = requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)}
plot(pcps, clades = 4, species_labels = FALSE)
```

The package PCPS also draws a curve of phylogenetic signal at the metacommunity level
(`pcps.curve()`), from regressions of community-weighted mean traits on an increasing number of
axes. In simulations by its authors, the curve of traits with low or high phylogenetic signal
did not depart from that expected under Brownian motion (Duarte et al. 2018), so it does not
measure the signal of the trait, and comdynamite does not implement it.

When sites are neighbours and the environment and the communities are both autocorrelated, free
permutations of sites reject far too often. `site_permutations` takes a restricted null model,
such as `torus_permutations()` on a complete grid, in `pcc_test()`, `phylo_beta_test()` and
`pcps_test()` alike. The help of `pcps_test()` gives the rates, including those in a landscape
with edges, where the torus still rejects too often when fields are broad.

## Reading the two p-values

All these functions permute sites, which breaks the link between composition and environment, and
species across the tips, which breaks the link between composition and phylogeny. The association
requires both links, so the p-value to report is `p_max`, the larger of the two. A small
`p_site` with a large `p_species` says that composition follows the environment, but that the
phylogeny adds nothing to it.

The scripts `data-raw/validation_pcc.R` and `data-raw/validation_phylo_beta.R` compare the
rejection rates of these tests with those published.

## Sites that are neighbours

Permutations of sites treat them as exchangeable. When they are neighbours, `site_permutations`
takes a restricted null model, such as those of `torus_permutations()` for a grid on a torus.
